name: BCH212 SA1 Mock Exam (Set 2)
subtitle: Lectures 1-9: Biomolecules, Enzymes, Bioenergetics & Metabolism
description: A second, entirely new full-length mock exam covering Lectures 1-9, with no repeated questions from the first mock exam set. Weighted by teaching hours to mirror the real Summative Assessment I distribution (4 questions per lecture hour).

questions.stem: The association of multiple folded polypeptide subunits into one functional protein complex (e.g., the four chains of haemoglobin) describes which level of protein structure?
options: Supersecondary structure
Quaternary structure
Tertiary structure
Primary structure
Secondary structure
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure refers specifically to proteins composed of two or more separate polypeptide chains (subunits) that associate non-covalently (or sometimes via disulfide bonds) into a single functional unit, such as haemoglobin's four globin subunits.

questions.stem: Disulfide bonds, which help stabilise the tertiary structure of many extracellular proteins, form through:
options: A condensation reaction between two carboxyl groups
Phosphorylation of a tyrosine residue
Hydrogen bonding between two serine residues
Glycosylation of an asparagine residue
Oxidation of two cysteine thiol (-SH) side chains to form a covalent -S-S- linkage
questions.explanation: Two cysteine residues, brought into proximity by protein folding, can be oxidised to form a covalent disulfide bond. This bond is especially common in secreted/extracellular proteins (e.g., insulin, antibodies), where the oxidising environment favours its formation and it adds extra structural stability.

questions.stem: Glucose and fructose are structural isomers that differ in that glucose is classified as an aldose while fructose is classified as a:
options: Deoxy sugar
Amino sugar
Ketose, because it contains a ketone functional group rather than an aldehyde
Diose
Sugar alcohol
questions.explanation: Aldoses (like glucose) have their carbonyl group as an aldehyde, typically at carbon 1, while ketoses (like fructose) have their carbonyl group as a ketone, typically at carbon 2 — this distinction affects their chemical reactivity and the ring structures they form.

questions.stem: Glucose and galactose are described as 'epimers' of each other because they:
options: Are identical compounds with different names
Differ at every chiral carbon
Differ in configuration at only a single chiral carbon (carbon 4)
Have different molecular formulas
Are non-carbohydrate isomers of one another
questions.explanation: Epimers are stereoisomers that differ in spatial configuration at exactly one of several chiral (stereogenic) centres. Glucose and galactose are both aldohexoses that differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group at carbon 4, making them C4 epimers.

questions.stem: The isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid is defined as the pH at which:
options: The molecule is maximally positively charged
The molecule is maximally negatively charged
The amino acid begins to denature
The peptide bond is hydrolysed
The molecule carries no net electrical charge (exists predominantly as a zwitterion)
questions.explanation: At the isoelectric point, the number of positive charges (protonated amino/side chain groups) exactly balances the number of negative charges (deprotonated carboxyl/side chain groups), giving the molecule zero net charge — important for techniques like isoelectric focusing.

questions.stem: Mutarotation refers to the phenomenon in which a freshly dissolved sugar:
options: Undergoes hydrolysis of its glycosidic bond
Becomes covalently linked to water
Is converted irreversibly into a different monosaccharide
Spontaneously interconverts between its alpha and beta anomeric forms via an open-chain intermediate
Permanently loses its ability to form a ring structure
questions.explanation: In solution, a cyclic monosaccharide can open to its linear form and re-close, potentially forming the opposite anomeric configuration (alpha or beta) at the anomeric carbon. This spontaneous equilibration, observable as a change in optical rotation over time, is called mutarotation.

questions.stem: According to Chargaff's rule, in double-stranded DNA the molar amount of adenine is equal to the molar amount of:
options: Uracil
Cytosine
Another adenine molecule on the same strand
Guanine
Thymine
questions.explanation: Chargaff's rule states that in double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so their molar quantities are equal (A=T, G=C) — an observation that provided key evidence for the base-pairing model of the DNA double helix.

questions.stem: The two strands of a DNA double helix run in opposite directions relative to one another, a property described as:
options: Parallel
Isomeric
Antiparallel
Semi-conservative
Perpendicular
questions.explanation: One DNA strand runs 5' to 3' while its complementary partner strand runs 3' to 5' in the same physical direction — this antiparallel arrangement is essential for correct base pairing and is a defining feature of the double helix.

questions.stem: The key structural difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide is that a nucleotide additionally contains:
options: An extra nitrogenous base
One or more phosphate groups
A peptide bond
An extra sugar molecule
A fatty acid chain
questions.explanation: A nucleoside consists only of a nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with one or more phosphate groups esterified to the sugar (typically at the 5' position), and nucleotides are the actual monomers polymerised into DNA and RNA.

questions.stem: A triglyceride (triacylglycerol) is formed by linking three fatty acid molecules to a glycerol backbone via which type of bond?
options: Phosphodiester bonds
Disulfide bonds
Amide bonds
Glycosidic bonds
Ester bonds
questions.explanation: Each of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups undergoes an esterification (condensation) reaction with the carboxyl group of a fatty acid, releasing water and forming an ester bond — triglycerides are the body's main storage form of fatty acids.

questions.stem: Cholesterol's characteristic four-ring steroid nucleus makes it the biosynthetic precursor for all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Bile acids
Cortisol
Vitamin D
Triglycerides
Estrogen
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is the common precursor for steroid hormones (cortisol, oestrogen, testosterone, aldosterone), bile acids, and vitamin D (via 7-dehydrocholesterol). Triglycerides, in contrast, are built from a glycerol backbone and fatty acids and are structurally and biosynthetically unrelated to the steroid nucleus.

questions.stem: Sphingomyelin, an important lipid component of the myelin sheath, is built on which backbone, distinguishing it from glycerophospholipids?
options: Sphingosine, an amino alcohol
Cholesterol
A fatty acid chain alone
Glycerol
Ribose
questions.explanation: Sphingolipids, including sphingomyelin, are built on a sphingosine backbone (a long-chain amino alcohol) rather than glycerol. Sphingomyelin specifically has a phosphocholine head group attached and is abundant in the myelin sheath surrounding nerve axons.

questions.stem: Enzymes increase the rate of a chemical reaction primarily by:
options: Lowering the activation energy required to reach the transition state, without changing the reaction's overall equilibrium
Increasing the total free energy released by the reaction
Supplying additional energy input to the reacting molecules
Permanently altering the structure of the substrate before catalysis begins
Shifting the equilibrium constant of the reaction toward products
questions.explanation: Enzymes provide an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, speeding up the approach to equilibrium in both the forward and reverse directions equally. They do not change the overall free energy change (delta-G) or equilibrium position of the reaction.

questions.stem: The 'induced fit' model of enzyme-substrate interaction proposes that:
options: The active site is a rigid, pre-formed shape that perfectly matches the substrate before binding
Binding occurs randomly with no conformational change in either molecule
The enzyme's active site changes shape upon substrate binding to achieve an optimal fit
The substrate must be chemically modified before it can bind the enzyme at all
Substrates change their own shape while the enzyme remains completely rigid
questions.explanation: Unlike the older rigid 'lock-and-key' model, the induced fit model (proposed by Koshland) suggests the enzyme's active site is somewhat flexible and undergoes a conformational change upon substrate binding, optimising the alignment of catalytic residues with the substrate.

questions.stem: Enzyme activity typically follows a bell-shaped curve with respect to pH and temperature because:
options: Substrate concentration always falls at extreme pH values
Cofactors are destroyed only at low temperatures, never at high temperatures
Only alkaline conditions ever affect enzyme structure
Extreme pH or temperature values progressively denature the enzyme, disrupting the conformation needed for catalysis
Enzymes function identically at every pH and temperature
questions.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimal pH and temperature at which its three-dimensional structure (and therefore activity) is best maintained. Moving away from these optima in either direction — but especially extreme values — progressively disrupts non-covalent interactions maintaining the enzyme's active conformation, reducing or abolishing activity (denaturation).

questions.stem: A prosthetic group differs from a loosely associating coenzyme in that a prosthetic group is:
options: Tightly, often covalently, bound to the enzyme on a permanent basis (e.g., FAD in succinate dehydrogenase)
Never required for catalytic activity
Always a metal ion rather than an organic molecule
Only found in enzymes lacking a protein component
Freely diffusible between different enzymes in the cell
questions.explanation: While some coenzymes (like NAD+) bind loosely and dissociate after each catalytic cycle, prosthetic groups (such as FAD, biotin, or haem) remain tightly and often covalently bound to their specific enzyme, functioning essentially as a permanent structural and functional component.

questions.stem: An uncompetitive inhibitor is distinguished from other reversible inhibitor types by the fact that it:
options: Requires an irreversible covalent bond to the active site
Binds only free enzyme and increases apparent Km while Vmax stays constant
Never affects the values of Km or Vmax
Binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex, decreasing both the apparent Km and Vmax
Binds an allosteric site, decreasing Vmax while Km stays constant
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors specifically bind the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex rather than the free enzyme, trapping it in an inactive form. This reduces both the apparent Vmax and the apparent Km (because the equilibrium is pulled toward more ES complex formation), a pattern distinguishable from competitive or simple noncompetitive inhibition on a Lineweaver-Burk plot.

questions.stem: Penicillin acts as a 'suicide' (mechanism-based) inhibitor of bacterial transpeptidase because it:
options: Is degraded by the enzyme without affecting its activity at all
Increases the enzyme's affinity for its natural substrate
Is processed by the enzyme's normal catalytic mechanism into a reactive form that then covalently and irreversibly inactivates it
Binds an allosteric site distant from the active site
Reversibly competes with the natural substrate at the active site
questions.explanation: Penicillin structurally resembles the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the bacterial cell wall precursor. The transpeptidase's own catalytic serine attacks penicillin's beta-lactam ring as if beginning a normal reaction, but this forms a stable, essentially irreversible covalent bond that permanently inactivates the enzyme.

questions.stem: On a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of 1/velocity versus 1/[substrate], the y-intercept of the plotted line corresponds to:
options: Km directly
The enzyme concentration
-1/Km
1/Vmax
Vmax directly
questions.explanation: The Lineweaver-Burk transformation of the Michaelis-Menten equation gives a straight line where the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax and the x-intercept equals -1/Km, allowing these kinetic parameters to be determined graphically from experimental data.

questions.stem: Lipases, which hydrolyse the ester bonds of triglycerides using a molecule of water, belong to which major enzyme class?
options: Hydrolases
Lyases
Oxidoreductases
Transferases
Isomerases
questions.explanation: Hydrolases (EC class 3) catalyse the cleavage of chemical bonds through the addition of a water molecule. Lipases specifically hydrolyse ester bonds in triglycerides, releasing free fatty acids and glycerol (or partial glycerides).

questions.stem: DNA ligase, which joins two DNA fragments together using energy from ATP or NAD+ hydrolysis, is classified as belonging to which major enzyme class?
options: Ligases
Hydrolases
Lyases
Isomerases
Transferases
questions.explanation: Ligases (EC class 6) catalyse the joining of two separate molecules into one, typically coupled to the hydrolysis of a high-energy bond (ATP or NAD+) to drive the otherwise unfavourable bond-forming reaction — DNA ligase sealing nicks in a DNA strand is a classic example.

questions.stem: A low Km value for a given enzyme-substrate pair generally indicates:
options: That the reaction is essentially irreversible
That the enzyme is saturated with substrate at all times
Low affinity of the enzyme for its substrate
That the enzyme requires a coenzyme to function
High affinity of the enzyme for its substrate (half-maximal velocity is reached at a low substrate concentration)
questions.explanation: Km is inversely related to substrate affinity under the standard Michaelis-Menten assumptions — a low Km means the enzyme reaches half its maximal rate at a low substrate concentration, implying the enzyme binds that substrate efficiently even when it is scarce.

questions.stem: Allosteric regulators (activators or inhibitors) of an enzyme typically exert their effect by:
options: Always binding at the exact same location as the substrate
Binding directly and exclusively to the substrate molecule itself
Covalently modifying the substrate before it reaches the enzyme
Permanently and irreversibly denaturing the enzyme
Binding a regulatory site distinct from the active site, inducing a conformational change that alters catalytic activity
questions.explanation: Allosteric regulation involves a small molecule binding at a site separate from the catalytic active site, triggering a conformational shift (often transmitted through subunit interactions in multimeric enzymes) that either enhances or reduces the enzyme's catalytic efficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a defining general property of essentially all biological enzymes?
options: They increase the rate of a specific reaction without being permanently consumed or altered in the overall process
They always require a metal ion cofactor to function
They are always consumed stoichiometrically in the reactions they catalyse
They can only catalyse reactions that are otherwise thermodynamically impossible
They function optimally only outside of physiological temperature and pH ranges
questions.explanation: As biological catalysts, enzymes accelerate specific reactions (often by many orders of magnitude) while emerging from the reaction chemically unchanged, ready to catalyse further rounds of the same reaction — though not every enzyme requires a metal cofactor, and none can make a thermodynamically unfavourable reaction spontaneously favourable.

questions.stem: ATP synthase generates ATP by harnessing the energy of:
options: Electron transfer occurring within the enzyme itself, without any proton involvement
Hydrolysis of NADH
Direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate molecule
A proton (H+) gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane flowing back into the matrix through the enzyme (chemiosmotic coupling)
Oxygen binding directly to ADP
questions.explanation: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the mitochondrial matrix, creating an electrochemical gradient (proton-motive force). ATP synthase acts as a molecular turbine, allowing protons to flow back down this gradient through it, and this flow drives the conformational changes that catalyse ATP synthesis from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

questions.stem: Substrate-level phosphorylation, exemplified by the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase reactions of glycolysis, is defined as:
options: Phosphorylation of a protein by a kinase enzyme as part of a signalling cascade
Any reaction that produces ADP from ATP
A reaction that occurs only within the mitochondrial matrix
The direct enzymatic transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate intermediate to ADP, independent of the electron transport chain
ATP synthesis driven exclusively by the proton gradient across a membrane
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation generates ATP (or GTP) through direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy phosphorylated substrate to ADP, catalysed by a specific enzyme — occurring in glycolysis and one step of the TCA cycle, entirely independent of oxygen, membrane gradients, or the electron transport chain.

questions.stem: A redox couple with a more positive (higher) standard reduction potential (E degree prime), compared to another couple, will tend to:
options: Never participate in electron transport chain reactions
Only participate in substrate-level phosphorylation reactions
Accept electrons from the couple with the lower (more negative) reduction potential
Remain chemically inert regardless of other couples present
Donate electrons to a couple with a higher reduction potential
questions.explanation: In the electron transport chain, electrons flow spontaneously from carriers with lower (more negative) standard reduction potentials toward carriers with higher (more positive) reduction potentials, ultimately reducing molecular oxygen (which has the highest reduction potential of the chain's components) to water.

questions.stem: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), the terminal complex of the electron transport chain, catalyses the transfer of electrons to which final acceptor?
options: Coenzyme Q, which is reduced to ubiquinol
Molecular oxygen, which is reduced to water
NAD+, which is reduced to NADH
Cytochrome c itself, in a closed loop
ADP, which is phosphorylated to ATP directly
questions.explanation: Complex IV accepts electrons from cytochrome c and uses them, along with protons from the matrix, to reduce molecular oxygen to water — the final electron-accepting step of the electron transport chain, and the reason the process is described as 'aerobic' respiration.

questions.stem: Because NADH donates its electrons at an earlier point in the electron transport chain than FADH2, oxidation of NADH is generally estimated to yield a higher:
options: P/O ratio (ATP produced per oxygen atom reduced, or per electron pair transferred)
Total number of oxygen molecules consumed per glucose oxidised
Amount of substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle
Rate of glycolysis
Standard reduction potential for oxygen itself
questions.explanation: Because NADH's electrons enter at Complex I (pumping protons there in addition to Complexes III and IV), while FADH2's electrons enter later at Complex II (bypassing Complex I's proton pumping), oxidation of NADH is associated with a higher P/O ratio (commonly cited as approximately 2.5 ATP) than FADH2 (approximately 1.5 ATP).

questions.stem: A thermodynamically unfavourable (endergonic) biochemical reaction can be made to proceed within the cell mainly by:
options: Coupling it to a favourable (exergonic) reaction, such as ATP hydrolysis, typically via a shared reaction intermediate
Converting the reaction into a purely physical (non-chemical) process
Lowering the temperature of the cell
Removing all cofactors from the reaction
Simply increasing the concentration of the enzyme catalysing it, with no other change
questions.explanation: Energetic coupling allows the large negative free energy change of a highly exergonic reaction (most commonly ATP hydrolysis) to be used to 'drive' a linked, otherwise unfavourable endergonic reaction forward, typically through a shared phosphorylated or otherwise activated intermediate — a strategy used throughout biosynthetic metabolism.

questions.stem: Hereditary orotic aciduria, presenting with megaloblastic anaemia unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folate and orotic acid crystals in the urine, results from deficiency of:
options: UMP synthase (the bifunctional enzyme with orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase activities)
Xanthine oxidase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
HGPRT
Adenosine deaminase
questions.explanation: UMP synthase catalyses the final two steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, converting orotic acid to UMP. Its deficiency causes orotic acid to accumulate and crystallise in urine, along with megaloblastic anaemia (due to impaired pyrimidine availability for nucleic acid synthesis) that does not respond to B12 or folate supplementation — distinguishing it from typical megaloblastic anaemias.

questions.stem: Ribonucleotide reductase, an essential and rate-limiting enzyme for DNA synthesis, catalyses the conversion of:
options: PRPP into ribose-5-phosphate
Purine bases into pyrimidine bases
Ribonucleoside diphosphates into their corresponding deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates
Uric acid into allantoin
Deoxyribonucleotides into ribonucleotides
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase removes the 2'-hydroxyl group from ribonucleoside diphosphates, generating the deoxyribonucleotides required for DNA replication and repair. It is a key target of certain chemotherapeutic agents, such as hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: Methotrexate, used both in cancer chemotherapy and in autoimmune disease treatment, exerts its effect by inhibiting:
options: DNA polymerase directly
Dihydrofolate reductase, blocking regeneration of tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis
Ribonucleotide reductase
Xanthine oxidase
Thymidylate synthase directly
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is a folate analogue that competitively and potently inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing regeneration of active tetrahydrofolate from dihydrofolate. Without adequate tetrahydrofolate, both thymidylate and purine synthesis are impaired, halting DNA replication in rapidly dividing cells.

questions.stem: The chemotherapeutic agent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) primarily exerts its cytotoxic effect on rapidly dividing cells by inhibiting:
options: Ribonucleotide reductase directly
Adenosine deaminase
Dihydrofolate reductase directly
HGPRT
Thymidylate synthase, after being converted intracellularly to FdUMP
questions.explanation: 5-FU is converted within cells to FdUMP, which forms a stable complex with thymidylate synthase (and the folate cofactor), irreversibly inhibiting the enzyme and blocking synthesis of dTMP — depriving rapidly dividing cells, including cancer cells, of thymidine needed for DNA replication.

questions.stem: PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate), synthesised from ribose-5-phosphate and ATP by PRPP synthetase, serves as a critical shared precursor for:
options: Only purine synthesis, never pyrimidine synthesis
Only the purine salvage pathway, not de novo synthesis
Both de novo purine and de novo pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis
Fatty acid synthesis exclusively
Only pyrimidine synthesis, never purine synthesis
questions.explanation: PRPP provides the activated ribose-phosphate unit used in both the purine (attaching to glutamine to begin the purine ring) and pyrimidine (attaching to orotate, generated separately) biosynthetic pathways, making it a central, shared metabolic branch point for nucleotide synthesis.

questions.stem: The purine salvage pathway, involving enzymes such as HGPRT and APRT, is metabolically important mainly because it:
options: Recycles free purine bases back into nucleotides, conserving energy compared to synthesising purines entirely from scratch
Is the only pathway capable of producing purine nucleotides in humans
Bypasses the need for PRPP entirely
Converts purines into pyrimidines for RNA synthesis
Produces uric acid directly as its main product
questions.explanation: Rather than rebuilding a purine ring from simple precursors (an energetically expensive, multi-step de novo process), salvage enzymes reattach free bases released from nucleic acid turnover (hypoxanthine, guanine, adenine) directly to PRPP, regenerating nucleotides far more efficiently — tissues like the brain rely heavily on salvage due to relatively low de novo synthesis capacity.

questions.stem: Compared to hexokinase, glucokinase (found mainly in the liver and pancreatic beta cells) is distinguished by having:
options: No ability to phosphorylate glucose at all
Identical kinetic properties to hexokinase in every tissue
Exclusive activity in skeletal muscle
A much higher Km for glucose and a lack of inhibition by glucose-6-phosphate
A much lower Km for glucose and strong inhibition by glucose-6-phosphate
questions.explanation: Glucokinase's high Km means its activity keeps increasing across the physiological range of blood glucose (rather than saturating early), and because it is not product-inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, it allows the liver and pancreatic beta cells to respond proportionally to blood glucose concentration — important for glucose sensing and hepatic glucose uptake after meals.

questions.stem: Hereditary fructose intolerance, in which ingestion of fructose can cause severe hypoglycaemia and liver damage, is caused by deficiency of:
options: Aldolase A
Aldolase B
Fructokinase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Galactokinase
questions.explanation: Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate in the liver. Its deficiency causes fructose-1-phosphate to accumulate after fructose ingestion, trapping intracellular phosphate and secondarily inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, producing severe hypoglycaemia and progressive liver injury with continued fructose exposure.

questions.stem: Classic galactosemia, presenting with failure to thrive, cataracts, and liver dysfunction in infants fed milk (which contains lactose), most commonly results from deficiency of:
options: Galactokinase
Aldolase B
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)
UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase
Lactase
questions.explanation: GALT deficiency prevents conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose, causing toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver, brain, kidney, and lens (contributing to cataracts). This is the classic, most severe form of galactosemia, requiring strict dietary galactose/lactose restriction.

questions.stem: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which interconverts pyruvate and lactate, is metabolically important during anaerobic glycolysis primarily because it:
options: Converts lactate into glucose within the same cell
Produces pyruvate for immediate entry into the TCA cycle
Is only active in the presence of abundant oxygen
Directly generates additional ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation
Regenerates NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue in the absence of adequate oxygen
questions.explanation: Under anaerobic conditions, the electron transport chain cannot efficiently reoxidise NADH. LDH allows glycolysis to continue by using excess NADH to reduce pyruvate to lactate, regenerating the NAD+ that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase requires to keep glycolytic flux going.

questions.stem: The branching enzyme involved in glycogen synthesis functions to:
options: Remove glucose units from the non-reducing ends of glycogen
Hydrolyse alpha-1,4 bonds exclusively
Convert glycogen directly into free glucose
Add a single primer glucose molecule to begin new glycogen synthesis
Create alpha-1,6 branch points, increasing the solubility of glycogen and the number of terminal ends available for rapid mobilisation
questions.explanation: Branching enzyme transfers a short oligosaccharide segment from the end of a growing glycogen chain and reattaches it via a new alpha-1,6 bond, creating a branch point. This increases both the solubility of the glycogen molecule and the number of non-reducing ends, from which glycogen phosphorylase can simultaneously act during rapid glycogenolysis.

questions.stem: The debranching enzyme, needed for complete breakdown of glycogen, primarily acts to:
options: Initiate new alpha-1,6 branch point formation
Convert glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate
Directly synthesise UDP-glucose
Add glucose residues to a growing glycogen chain
Remove the alpha-1,6 branch points remaining after glycogen phosphorylase has removed the outer branches
questions.explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase can only remove glucose units from alpha-1,4 linkages up to about four residues from a branch point. The debranching enzyme (with its transferase and alpha-1,6-glucosidase activities) then relocates the remaining residues and cleaves the branch point, allowing complete glycogen breakdown.

questions.stem: Complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation combined) yields substantially more ATP than anaerobic glycolysis alone, with modern estimates placing the total net yield at approximately:
options: 4 ATP
8 ATP
2 ATP
60 ATP
questions.explanation: While anaerobic glycolysis alone nets only 2 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation, complete aerobic oxidation captures far more energy through oxidative phosphorylation of the NADH and FADH2 generated at multiple steps, with contemporary P/O ratio estimates giving a total net yield of approximately 30-32 ATP per glucose (older textbooks using higher, less precise P/O ratios cite 36-38).

questions.stem: The non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway, involving transketolase and transaldolase reactions, primarily functions to:
options: Synthesise fatty acids from acetyl-CoA
Produce ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation
Directly oxidise glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate
Generate the majority of the pathway's NADPH output
Interconvert various sugar phosphates, allowing production of ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis (or, alternatively, feeding intermediates back into glycolysis)
questions.explanation: Unlike the oxidative phase (which irreversibly generates NADPH), the non-oxidative phase reversibly interconverts 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 7-carbon sugar phosphates, allowing the cell to flexibly produce ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleotide synthesis) when NADPH demand is low, or to feed excess pentose phosphates back into glycolytic intermediates when nucleotide synthesis needs are low.

questions.stem: In the liver, fructokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, allowing fructose metabolism to largely bypass which key regulatory step of glycolysis?
options: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
Aldolase B itself
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Pyruvate kinase only
Hexokinase only, with no effect on PFK-1
questions.explanation: Because fructose-1-phosphate is cleaved by aldolase B directly into glycolytic triose intermediates without needing to pass through the tightly regulated PFK-1 step, dietary fructose can enter glycolysis more rapidly and with less regulatory control than glucose, which is thought to contribute to fructose's greater tendency to promote lipogenesis when consumed in excess.

questions.stem: Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III), generally milder than Von Gierke disease, is caused by deficiency of:
options: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase
Debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase)
Branching enzyme
questions.explanation: In Cori disease, glycogen with abnormally short outer branches accumulates because the debranching enzyme cannot remove the branch points. Because glycogen phosphorylase can still act on the outer branches (unlike in Von Gierke disease, where glucose-6-phosphatase itself is absent), symptoms including hypoglycaemia are generally less severe.

questions.stem: Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II), characterised by cardiomegaly and profound muscle weakness in infancy, results from deficiency of:
options: Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase)
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Cytoplasmic glycogen phosphorylase
Glycogen synthase
Debranching enzyme
questions.explanation: Pompe disease is unique among the glycogen storage diseases in being a lysosomal storage disorder — acid alpha-glucosidase normally degrades glycogen within lysosomes, and its absence causes massive lysosomal glycogen accumulation, particularly damaging to cardiac and skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: Pyruvate carboxylase, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate as the first committed step of gluconeogenesis, requires which vitamin-derived cofactor and is allosterically activated by which molecule?
options: Niacin as cofactor; allosterically inhibited by acetyl-CoA
Folate as cofactor; allosterically activated by AMP
Vitamin B12 as cofactor; allosterically activated by citrate
Thiamine as cofactor; allosterically activated by ATP
Biotin as cofactor; allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA
questions.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent carboxylase. It is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA — when acetyl-CoA accumulates (signalling abundant fuel from fatty acid oxidation), this stimulates oxaloacetate formation, replenishing the TCA cycle and supporting gluconeogenesis during fasting.

questions.stem: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), formed from methionine and ATP, functions in the cell mainly as:
options: An essential amino acid used only for protein synthesis
The universal methyl group donor for numerous methylation reactions (DNA, proteins, neurotransmitters, phospholipids)
A cofactor exclusively for transamination reactions
A direct precursor of urea
The primary carrier of one-carbon units derived from folate
questions.explanation: SAM's activated methyl group (made highly reactive by the adjacent positively charged sulfonium ion) is transferred by methyltransferase enzymes to a wide variety of acceptor molecules, including DNA (epigenetic methylation), phospholipids, and neurotransmitter precursors (e.g., in catecholamine synthesis).

questions.stem: Alkaptonuria, characterised by urine that darkens on standing and later joint/cartilage pigmentation (ochronosis), results from deficiency of:
options: Tyrosinase
Phenylalanine hydroxylase
Cystathionine beta-synthase
Homogentisate oxidase
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: Homogentisate oxidase normally further degrades homogentisic acid in the tyrosine catabolic pathway. Its absence causes homogentisic acid to accumulate and oxidise/polymerise upon exposure to air (darkening urine) and to deposit in connective tissue over years, producing the bluish-black pigmentation of ochronosis.

questions.stem: Nitrogen balance is used clinically to assess protein nutritional status by comparing:
options: Serum albumin concentration alone
Urinary creatinine excretion alone
Total caloric intake against total caloric expenditure
Total nitrogen intake (mainly from dietary protein) against total nitrogen excretion (mainly as urea)
Blood glucose levels before and after a protein meal
questions.explanation: A positive nitrogen balance (intake exceeds excretion) reflects net protein synthesis/tissue growth, as seen in children, pregnancy, or recovery from illness. A negative nitrogen balance (excretion exceeds intake) reflects net protein breakdown, as seen in starvation, severe burns, or critical illness.

questions.stem: Leucine and lysine are classified as purely 'ketogenic' amino acids because their carbon skeletons are degraded exclusively to:
options: Succinyl-CoA only
Pyruvate, allowing full conversion to glucose
Alpha-ketoglutarate only
Oxaloacetate, a direct gluconeogenic precursor
Acetyl-CoA and/or acetoacetyl-CoA, with no net contribution to glucose synthesis
questions.explanation: Unlike glucogenic amino acids (degraded to pyruvate or TCA cycle intermediates that can be net converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis), leucine and lysine yield only acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA, which cannot undergo net conversion to glucose, making them purely ketogenic — capable of contributing to ketone body or fatty acid synthesis but not to new glucose production.

questions.stem: N-acetylglutamate, synthesised from acetyl-CoA and glutamate, plays an essential regulatory role in nitrogen metabolism by:
options: Serving as the immediate nitrogen donor for arginine synthesis
Acting as a competitive inhibitor of glutamate dehydrogenase
Acting as an obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme of the urea cycle
Inhibiting the urea cycle when amino acid intake is high
Directly detoxifying ammonia into urea without any enzyme involvement
questions.explanation: Without N-acetylglutamate bound, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) has very low activity. Rising amino acid catabolism increases glutamate and acetyl-CoA availability, raising N-acetylglutamate synthesis, which activates CPS I and appropriately increases urea cycle capacity to match the nitrogen load requiring disposal.

questions.stem: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, the most common urea cycle disorder, causes hyperammonemia along with a distinctive additional finding of:
options: Markedly reduced serum ammonia levels
Elevated plasma phenylalanine
Orotic aciduria, because accumulating carbamoyl phosphate is shunted into the cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis pathway
Hypoglycaemia as the dominant presenting feature
Severe megaloblastic anaemia unresponsive to vitamin therapy
questions.explanation: When OTC (which normally combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine within the mitochondria) is deficient, the mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate that accumulates can leak into the cytosol and enter the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, where it is converted to orotic acid — producing orotic aciduria alongside the hyperammonemia, a useful distinguishing clinical clue (unlike the earlier-described UMP synthase deficiency, where orotic aciduria occurs without hyperammonemia).

questions.stem: Arginine serves as the direct biochemical precursor for synthesis of which important signalling molecule, via the enzyme nitric oxide synthase?
options: Nitric oxide (NO)
Dopamine
Serotonin
Carbon monoxide
Histamine
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine (using molecular oxygen and NADPH) into nitric oxide and citrulline. NO is a short-lived signalling gas important in vascular smooth muscle relaxation (vasodilation), neurotransmission, and immune defence.

questions.stem: Creatine, whose phosphorylated form (phosphocreatine) serves as a rapid energy buffer in muscle, is synthesised from which combination of amino acids?
options: Only cysteine and methionine
Only glycine and serine
Only lysine and leucine
Arginine, glycine, and methionine
Only phenylalanine and tyrosine
questions.explanation: Creatine synthesis begins with a transfer of the guanidino group from arginine to glycine (forming guanidinoacetate), which is then methylated using a methyl group donated by S-adenosylmethionine (derived from methionine) to form creatine — phosphocreatine can then rapidly regenerate ATP during short bursts of intense muscle activity.

questions.stem: Histamine, an important mediator of allergic and inflammatory responses, is synthesised directly from which amino acid via a PLP-dependent decarboxylation reaction?
options: Arginine
Tryptophan
Histidine
Tyrosine
Glutamate
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylase, a pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6)-dependent enzyme, removes the carboxyl group from histidine to directly produce histamine, which is then stored in mast cell and basophil granules for release during allergic or inflammatory reactions.

questions.stem: Tryptophan serves as the metabolic precursor for both the neurotransmitter serotonin and, via the kynurenine pathway, for endogenous synthesis of which vitamin?
options: Biotin (Vitamin B7)
Niacin (Vitamin B3)
Riboflavin (Vitamin B2)
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
Folate (Vitamin B9)
questions.explanation: In addition to being hydroxylated and decarboxylated to form serotonin, a portion of dietary tryptophan is degraded via the kynurenine pathway to quinolinic acid, which can be converted into niacin (NAD+/NADP+ precursor) — though this conversion is inefficient, requiring roughly 60 mg of tryptophan to generate just 1 mg of niacin.

questions.stem: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyses the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of which group of neurotransmitters/hormones from tyrosine?
options: Histamine
GABA
Thyroid hormones exclusively, with no role in catecholamine synthesis
Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine)
Serotonin and melatonin
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to L-DOPA, the first and rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis. L-DOPA is subsequently decarboxylated to dopamine, which can be further converted to norepinephrine and then epinephrine in the appropriate tissues (e.g., adrenal medulla).

questions.stem: The transsulfuration pathway allows the body to synthesise cysteine using sulfur ultimately derived from which essential amino acid?
options: Phenylalanine
Lysine
Methionine
Valine
Threonine
questions.explanation: In the transsulfuration pathway, homocysteine (derived from methionine after donating its methyl group as SAM) condenses with serine, catalysed by cystathionine beta-synthase, to form cystathionine, which is then cleaved by cystathionase to yield cysteine — this allows methionine's sulfur atom to be repurposed for cysteine synthesis, making cysteine conditionally non-essential provided adequate methionine is available.

questions.stem: Each single cycle of mitochondrial beta-oxidation shortens the fatty acyl-CoA chain by two carbons (released as acetyl-CoA) while also generating:
options: One molecule of NADPH only
Two molecules of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation
Two molecules of NADH only
One molecule of NADH and one molecule of FADH2
Four molecules of CO2
questions.explanation: Each cycle of beta-oxidation involves four sequential reactions (an FAD-dependent oxidation, hydration, an NAD+-dependent oxidation, and thiolytic cleavage), together producing one FADH2, one NADH, and one acetyl-CoA per cycle, which then feed into the electron transport chain and TCA cycle respectively.

questions.stem: The multi-domain cytosolic enzyme fatty acid synthase uses NADPH (rather than NADH) as its reducing agent to synthesise which end product from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA units?
options: Ketone bodies
Arachidonic acid directly
Cholesterol
Glycerol-3-phosphate
Palmitate, a 16-carbon saturated fatty acid
questions.explanation: Fatty acid synthase repeatedly adds two-carbon units (derived from malonyl-CoA) to a growing acyl chain, using NADPH (mainly supplied by the pentose phosphate pathway) for the two reduction steps in each elongation cycle, ultimately releasing palmitate (C16:0) as its principal direct product.

questions.stem: VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein) particles are assembled and secreted by the liver primarily to transport:
options: Endogenously synthesised triglycerides (and some cholesterol) to peripheral tissues
Excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver
Bile acids to the gallbladder
Dietary triglycerides absorbed directly from the intestine
Free amino acids to muscle tissue
questions.explanation: While chylomicrons handle dietary (exogenous) fat, VLDL is the liver's vehicle for exporting triglycerides synthesised endogenously (e.g., from excess dietary carbohydrate converted to fat), delivering them to adipose and muscle tissue; VLDL is progressively converted to IDL and then LDL as its triglyceride content is depleted by lipoprotein lipase.

questions.stem: ApoB-48, the structural apolipoprotein found in chylomicrons, is related to ApoB-100 (found in VLDL/LDL) in that it is:
options: A degradation product of mature LDL particles
The fully glycosylated version of ApoB-100
A completely unrelated protein encoded by a separate gene
Produced only in the liver, identically to ApoB-100
A truncated form of the same gene product, produced in the intestine through mRNA editing that introduces a premature stop codon
questions.explanation: The apolipoprotein B gene is identical in liver and intestine, but intestinal cells edit the mRNA (via the enzyme APOBEC1) to introduce a premature stop codon, producing the shorter ApoB-48 (48% of the full length) found specifically in chylomicrons, while the liver produces the full-length ApoB-100 for VLDL.

questions.stem: ApoC-II, a small apolipoprotein carried on chylomicrons and VLDL, is functionally important because it:
options: Mediates clearance of chylomicron remnants by the liver
Inhibits cholesterol synthesis in the liver
Directly transports fat-soluble vitamins in the bloodstream
Binds the LDL receptor to mediate cholesterol uptake by peripheral cells
Activates lipoprotein lipase at the capillary endothelium, enabling hydrolysis of the particle's triglyceride core
questions.explanation: ApoC-II is transferred to nascent chylomicrons and VLDL from HDL and serves as an essential cofactor that activates lipoprotein lipase on the capillary endothelium of adipose tissue and muscle, permitting hydrolysis of the triglycerides carried within these lipoproteins.

questions.stem: ApoE, another key apolipoprotein, functions mainly to mediate:
options: Direct inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase
Binding of chylomicrons to intestinal brush border cells
Cholesterol esterification within HDL particles
Activation of lipoprotein lipase at the capillary endothelium
Hepatic receptor-mediated clearance of chylomicron remnants and IDL particles from the circulation
questions.explanation: After lipoprotein lipase removes most of the triglyceride from chylomicrons and VLDL, the resulting remnant particles (chylomicron remnants and IDL) are recognised by hepatic receptors via ApoE, allowing their efficient clearance from the circulation by the liver.

questions.stem: PCSK9, a protein secreted mainly by the liver and the target of a newer class of cholesterol-lowering drugs, raises plasma LDL cholesterol by:
options: Binding LDL receptors and promoting their degradation, reducing the liver's capacity to clear LDL from the blood
Inhibiting bile acid synthesis from cholesterol
Activating lipoprotein lipase excessively
Increasing intestinal cholesterol absorption directly
Directly inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase
questions.explanation: Normally, LDL receptors are recycled back to the cell surface after delivering LDL particles for endocytosis. PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor and redirects it toward lysosomal degradation instead of recycling; PCSK9 inhibitor drugs block this interaction, allowing more LDL receptors to remain available and lowering plasma LDL cholesterol.

questions.stem: Bile acids facilitate the intestinal absorption of dietary fat mainly through their ability to:
options: Convert cholesterol into bile pigments
Activate pancreatic amylase
Emulsify fat and form mixed micelles with fatty acids and monoglycerides, aiding their transport across the intestinal brush border
Directly stimulate hepatic VLDL secretion
Directly hydrolyse triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: As amphipathic molecules, bile acids surround partially digested lipids (fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol) to form small, soluble mixed micelles within the aqueous intestinal lumen, greatly increasing the surface area and effective solubility of these lipids so they can diffuse to and across the enterocyte brush border for absorption.

questions.stem: Very-long-chain fatty acids (typically greater than 20-22 carbons), which cannot be efficiently processed by standard mitochondrial beta-oxidation, are instead initially oxidised within:
options: The nucleus
Lysosomes
The rough endoplasmic reticulum
The Golgi apparatus
Peroxisomes
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes perform an initial round of beta-oxidation on very-long-chain fatty acids, shortening them before the remaining chain is transferred to mitochondria for completion. Zellweger syndrome, caused by defective peroxisome biogenesis, results in toxic accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids.

questions.stem: Beta-oxidation of an odd-chain-length fatty acid ultimately generates a final three-carbon propionyl-CoA unit (rather than only two-carbon acetyl-CoA units), which is then converted, via a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme, into:
options: Pyruvate directly, bypassing the TCA cycle
Oxaloacetate directly, without any intermediate steps
Glucose directly
Succinyl-CoA, which can enter the TCA cycle
Additional acetyl-CoA directly
questions.explanation: Propionyl-CoA is first carboxylated (a biotin-dependent step) to methylmalonyl-CoA, which is then isomerised by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase — a reaction requiring vitamin B12 (as adenosylcobalamin) as cofactor — into succinyl-CoA, allowing odd-chain fatty acid carbons to be anaplerotically incorporated into the TCA cycle.

questions.stem: Elongation of fatty acid chains beyond the 16-carbon palmitate product of fatty acid synthase, as well as introduction of double bonds by desaturase enzymes, occurs primarily within:
options: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum
The cytosol, using the same fatty acid synthase complex
The nucleus
The mitochondrial matrix
The peroxisome exclusively
questions.explanation: Unlike the initial de novo synthesis of palmitate (a cytosolic process using fatty acid synthase), further elongation and desaturation of fatty acids are carried out by separate enzyme systems located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, allowing production of longer-chain and unsaturated fatty acid species.

questions.stem: Adipocytes have very low glycerol kinase activity, meaning that triglyceride synthesis (esterification of fatty acids) within fat cells requires glycerol-3-phosphate to be generated instead primarily from:
options: Free glycerol released during lipolysis, directly re-phosphorylated by the same cell
Cholesterol synthesis intermediates
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate, an intermediate of glucose metabolism (glycolysis)
Ketone body metabolism
Amino acid catabolism exclusively
questions.explanation: Because adipocytes lack significant glycerol kinase activity, they cannot efficiently reuse free glycerol released during lipolysis for new triglyceride synthesis. Instead, they rely on glycolysis-derived dihydroxyacetone phosphate, reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate, to provide the backbone for esterifying fatty acids into new triglycerides — a process highly dependent on adequate glucose availability and insulin signalling.

questions.stem: The insulin receptor initiates its intracellular signalling cascade by functioning as a:
options: Receptor tyrosine kinase, which autophosphorylates and then phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins
G-protein coupled receptor that activates adenylate cyclase
Receptor with no intrinsic enzymatic activity of its own
Ligand-gated ion channel
Nuclear steroid hormone receptor
questions.explanation: Insulin binding activates the receptor's intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, leading to autophosphorylation and subsequent phosphorylation of IRS proteins, which recruit and activate downstream signalling molecules (including PI3K and Akt) that mediate insulin's diverse metabolic effects, including GLUT4 translocation to the cell membrane.

questions.stem: In contrast to the insulin receptor, the glucagon receptor on hepatocytes signals through which mechanism?
options: A ligand-gated calcium channel
As a G-protein coupled receptor that activates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP and activating protein kinase A
Direct activation of nuclear transcription factors without any second messenger
Intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, similar to the insulin receptor
Direct phosphorylation of glycogen by the receptor itself
questions.explanation: Glucagon binds a Gs-protein coupled receptor, activating adenylate cyclase and raising cAMP, which in turn activates protein kinase A (PKA) — PKA then phosphorylates numerous target enzymes (e.g., glycogen phosphorylase kinase, hormone-sensitive lipase) to coordinate the fasting metabolic response.

questions.stem: During the first several hours of fasting (the early post-absorptive state), the predominant source maintaining blood glucose is:
options: Ketone body utilisation by the brain
Dietary glucose still being absorbed from the intestine
Gluconeogenesis from muscle protein breakdown
Hepatic glycogenolysis (breakdown of liver glycogen stores)
Renal gluconeogenesis exclusively
questions.explanation: In the first several hours after a meal, liver glycogen stores are the primary and most readily mobilised source of glucose to maintain blood glucose levels. As fasting continues beyond roughly 24 hours and glycogen stores become depleted, gluconeogenesis progressively becomes the dominant source.

questions.stem: As fasting progresses beyond glycogen depletion (roughly 24-48 hours), the body increasingly relies on gluconeogenesis using which combination of substrates?
options: Only free fatty acids, converted directly to glucose
Only ketone bodies, converted directly to glucose
Only dietary carbohydrate absorbed from a recent meal
Amino acids (particularly alanine and glutamine), lactate, and glycerol
Cholesterol, converted directly to glucose
questions.explanation: Once hepatic glycogen is exhausted, gluconeogenesis becomes essential, drawing on amino acids released from muscle protein breakdown (especially alanine and glutamine), lactate (from red blood cell and muscle glycolysis), and glycerol (from adipose tissue lipolysis) as carbon sources — notably, fatty acids and ketone bodies cannot be net converted to glucose in humans.

questions.stem: The glucose-alanine cycle describes an inter-organ metabolic relationship in which:
options: The kidney is the primary site of alanine production
Muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine (using amino groups from protein breakdown) and exports it to the liver for gluconeogenesis and urea synthesis
Muscle directly converts alanine into glucose without any liver involvement
Alanine is converted into glycogen within the muscle itself
Liver exports alanine to muscle for direct use as an energy source
questions.explanation: During fasting or exercise, muscle protein breakdown releases amino acids; their amino groups are transferred (via transamination) onto pyruvate to form alanine, which travels through the blood to the liver. There, alanine is transaminated back to pyruvate (a gluconeogenic substrate), while the liberated amino group is disposed of via the urea cycle — effectively shuttling both carbon skeletons and nitrogen from muscle to liver in a non-toxic form.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, epinephrine helps mobilise fuel for working muscle mainly by simultaneously stimulating:
options: Intestinal absorption of dietary glucose
Only renal gluconeogenesis, with no effect on the liver or adipose tissue
Hepatic glycogen synthesis and adipose tissue lipogenesis
Hepatic glycogenolysis and adipose tissue lipolysis
Insulin secretion from the pancreas
questions.explanation: Epinephrine released during exercise acts on both the liver (stimulating glycogen phosphorylase via the cAMP-PKA pathway to release glucose) and adipose tissue (stimulating hormone-sensitive lipase to release free fatty acids), together increasing the availability of both major fuel substrates for contracting muscle.

questions.stem: Leptin, secreted by adipose tissue roughly in proportion to fat mass, signals long-term energy status to the hypothalamus mainly to:
options: Directly stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells
Increase appetite and decrease energy expenditure
Directly inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis
Stimulate glycogen breakdown in skeletal muscle
Suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure when fat stores are adequate
questions.explanation: Leptin acts as an adipostat signal — as fat mass and leptin levels rise, hypothalamic signalling reduces appetite and increases energy expenditure, tending to limit further fat gain. Leptin resistance (rather than deficiency) is thought to contribute to obesity in most humans, since leptin levels are usually already elevated in obese individuals.

questions.stem: Excess thyroid hormone (T3) broadly affects metabolism mainly by:
options: Having no significant effect on overall energy expenditure
Selectively inhibiting only lipid metabolism, with no effect on carbohydrates or proteins
Decreasing mitochondrial oxygen consumption
Increasing basal metabolic rate and stimulating turnover of carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism generally
Acting exclusively on the pancreas to increase insulin secretion
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone broadly upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism across many tissues, increasing basal metabolic rate and accelerating both catabolic (e.g., lipolysis, protein breakdown) and anabolic pathways — explaining the weight loss, heat intolerance, and increased appetite characteristic of hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: Growth hormone opposes several of insulin's metabolic actions, an effect sometimes described as 'diabetogenic,' primarily by:
options: Promoting glycogen synthesis identically to insulin
Directly increasing pancreatic insulin secretion
Inhibiting protein synthesis and promoting muscle wasting
Promoting lipolysis and reducing peripheral tissue glucose uptake in response to insulin
Suppressing hepatic glucose output entirely
questions.explanation: Growth hormone stimulates lipolysis (raising free fatty acids, which themselves impair insulin sensitivity via the Randle cycle) and reduces glucose uptake in muscle and fat, effectively antagonising insulin's glucose-lowering actions, while separately promoting protein synthesis and growth largely via IGF-1.

questions.stem: Insulin resistance, a central feature of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome, is best defined as a state in which:
options: Target tissues (muscle, fat, liver) show a reduced metabolic response to a given circulating insulin concentration, requiring higher insulin levels to achieve normal glucose handling
Blood glucose is always below the normal range
Insulin is degraded immediately upon release, before reaching any tissue
The pancreas has completely stopped producing insulin
Insulin receptors are entirely absent from all tissues
questions.explanation: In insulin resistance, insulin signalling within target cells is blunted (often due to defects in the post-receptor signalling cascade), so a normal or even elevated insulin concentration produces a smaller-than-expected biological effect. The pancreas typically compensates initially by secreting more insulin (hyperinsulinaemia), but beta-cell function may eventually decline, leading to overt hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: Metabolic syndrome is defined by the co-occurrence of a cluster of conditions that together increase cardiovascular risk, generally including insulin resistance/hyperglycaemia, central obesity, dyslipidaemia, and:
options: Hyperthyroidism
Hypertension
Iron deficiency anaemia
Chronic kidney disease as a defining criterion
Hypocalcaemia
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome is typically diagnosed based on a combination of central (abdominal) obesity, elevated fasting glucose or insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia (elevated triglycerides and/or low HDL cholesterol), and elevated blood pressure (hypertension) — together substantially increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: SREBP (sterol regulatory element-binding protein), a transcription factor activated when intracellular cholesterol levels are low, upregulates transcription of genes such as:
options: Glycogen synthase exclusively
HMG-CoA reductase, promoting increased cholesterol synthesis
Beta-oxidation enzymes exclusively
Urea cycle enzymes exclusively
Glucose-6-phosphatase exclusively
questions.explanation: When cellular cholesterol is low, SREBP is released from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, transported to the Golgi for proteolytic activation, and moves to the nucleus, where it binds sterol regulatory elements to increase transcription of genes for cholesterol synthesis (including HMG-CoA reductase) and LDL receptor expression, restoring adequate cellular cholesterol supply.
